title: LLMS ON TRIAL: EVALUATING JUDICIAL FAIRNESS FOR LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS

bias_targets.methodology: Counterfactual prompting by altering the gender of the defendant, victim, or legal professionals (defender, prosecutor, judge) in judicial case descriptions, followed by regression analysis on the predicted sentence length.
Counterfactual prompting by altering the sexual orientation of involved parties in case descriptions, evaluating the systematic impact on predicted sentence lengths.
Counterfactual substitution of the ethnicity (e.g., Han vs. Ethnic Minority) of involved parties in the prompts, measuring the effect on predicted sentences.
Modifying the age of the defendant, victim, or legal professionals in prompts to observe systematic shifts in predicted sentence length.
Replacing the education level of involved parties in case descriptions and analyzing the resulting changes in LLM sentencing decisions.
Altering the occupation (e.g., farmer, worker, unemployed) of parties in the prompts to measure sentencing bias.
Counterfactual prompting by varying the financial status/wealth (e.g., penniless vs. millionaire) of involved parties to assess bias in sentencing.
Substituting the religious beliefs of parties in case descriptions to evaluate systematic differences in model judicial judgments.
Modifying the political background (e.g., CCP member vs. general masses) of parties to measure the impact on judicial decisions.
Altering the nationality (e.g., Chinese vs. Foreigner) of parties in prompts and evaluating the effect on predicted sentences.
Counterfactually changing the household registration status (local vs. non-local/rural vs. urban) of parties to measure geographic or systemic sentencing disparities.

Altering non-demographic procedural and extra-legal factors (e.g., court level, crime time/location, trial openness, legal representation type) in prompts to measure their unwarranted influence on LLM sentencing.
